title: Eisenkot navigates tricky waters as he tests power-sharing with Netanyahu
summary: Some of his allies are calling for such an arrangement, but it would represent a betrayal of his pre-election promise.

Listen (5 mins) Save Share Eisenkot navigates tricky waters as he tests power-sharing with Netanyahu on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Eisenkot looks on as he arrives at the Israeli parliament, or Knesset, in West Jerusalem, November 10, 2026 [AFP] By Nour Odeh Published On 27 Nov 2026 27 Nov 2026 The 2026 Israeli elections were termed the most consequential in recent decades for the country – for multiple reasons. For Benjamin Netanyahu, the caretaker prime minister, and his right-wing coalition, the elections were about keeping the far-right in power to protect the formative changes they enacted in state policies and institutions. For the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot – or the “change bloc”, as it is referred to – the promise was to replace the failed October 7 government as they termed it, rehabilitate Israel’s international standing, and end internal divisions. Once the results were announced, things changed. Gadi Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel’s next government. But his bloc does not have enough seats in the Knesset to win a vote of confidence on its own. The United Arab List and the Joint List, parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, have 19 seats and are willing to back Eisenkot in his efforts to replace Netanyahu as Israel’s premier. But some in the change bloc, such as Avigdor Lieberman , promised not to support any government coalition that includes an Arab-led party or one that depended on votes from Palestinian citizens of Israel. This, despite the fact that Lieberman himself became chair of the Knesset’s Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee thanks to those same votes. That contradiction was pointed out by Mohamed Majadli, the chief editor of AlNas Radio in Israel and an analyst on the country’s Channel 12. In such a limited space for political manoeuvres, Eisenkot embarked on forming a coalition, holding talks with his partners, while also trying to open channels of communication with ultra-Orthodox parties, particularly the United Torah Judaism party. At the same time, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett led efforts to form a unity government with Netanyahu’s Likud party and succeeded in convincing Eisenkot’s Yashar party to open formal talks with Likud. Advertisement The prospect of reneging on the change bloc’s central promise to oust Netanyahu looms large over these talks. Bennett and others are advocating for that outcome in light of the lack of a clear Zionist majority against Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. Meanwhile, leader of the Democrats group, Yair Golan, has publicly opposed any unity formula with Netanyahu and has called out Bennett for his efforts to reach it. The Yashar-Likud talks are complex and overshadowed by, among other issues, accusations between the two sides. Netanyahu accuses the change bloc of working to undermine Israel by working with Arab-led parties, which he has referred to as “the enemy”. Eisenkot has gone on the record saying that Netanyahu endangers the security of Israel and is willing to ignite war for his personal gain. From Likud’s perspective, a unity government would require a rotation agreement on the premiership. That means that rather than getting rid of Netanyahu, Eisenkot would have to agree to Netanyahu staying on as prime minister for two years, or agreeing to serve second in the rotation. This scenario gained traction after judges presiding over Netanyahu corruption trials recommended dropping the most serious charge of bribery, as well as reconsidering the charges or reaching a plea bargain in the others. This development has strengthened Netanyahu’s negotiating position and prompted him to call for an end to the political boycott against him. Against this backdrop, Eisenkot is manoeuvring through dangerous political waters. If he fails to form a government, voters may be forced to return to the polls again while Netanyahu remains at the helm. This scenario could translate into a loss of support for the change bloc and hand Netanyahu a renewed mandate, while simultaneously ending the political careers of some leaders such as Eisenkot. If Eisenkot chooses unity with Netanyahu over the promises he made to his voters, he will lose credibility among supporters. Additionally, Eisenkot could be outmanoeuvred by Netanyahu. Many point to the coalition agreement between Benjamin Netanyahu and Benny Gantz in 2020, which included a rotating premiership. The government collapsed before Benny Gantz assumed his position and his political career never recovered. In political terms, forming a unity government with Netanyahu would represent a reversal of election promises on fundamental issues such as transparency, judicial reform, and the influence of religion on the state, because unlike the change bloc, Netanyahu’s allies are already embedded in the state bureaucracy and able to entrench these policies.
